original_question: Let A_n(t) be the polynomial sequence defined by (n^3 - (-1)^n t^3) A_n(t) + (n+1)^2(2n+1) A_{n+1}(t) + ((n+2)^2/(n+1)) A_{n+2}(t) = 0 with A_0 = 1 and A_1 = 0, and let A_tilde_n(t) = sum_{k=0}^n A_k(t). If A_tilde_n satisfies (n^3 - (-1)^n t^3) A_tilde_{n-1} + (2n+1)n A_tilde_n - (n+1)^2 n A_tilde_{n+1} = 0, is there an argument that deduces directly from this recurrence that lim_{n->infinity} A_tilde_n(t) = product over j>=1 of (1 + t^3/(8 j^3))?
target_in_paper: Section 7, Question 7.1 (first sentence) of arXiv:1607.06196; the notation and detailed recurrence background are supplied by Section 5 of reference [43] there, namely arXiv:1504.07696.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly targets the first half of Question 7.1: the recurrence-based proof of the limit for the partial sums A_tilde_n(t). It also correctly uses the equivalent reformulation in terms of A_tilde_n(t)=sum_{k=0}^n A_k(t), gives the right three-term recurrence for A_tilde_n, and identifies the right limiting product product_{j>=1}(1+t^3/(8 j^3)).
missing_details: The exact target in the specified paper is an open problem, Question 7.1 in Section 7, not a theorem or conjecture.
The defining recurrence for A_n(t) has coefficient (n+2)^2(n+1) in front of A_{n+2}(t), not (n+2)^2/(n+1).
To be paper-faithful and stand-alone, one should state that A_n(t), and hence A_tilde_n(t), lie in Q[t^3]; viewed as polynomials in x=t^3, they have degree floor(n/2).
The recurrence for A_tilde_n(t) is indexed for n=1,2,3,... .
The paper’s point is not to re-prove the product identity by external multiple-zeta-value methods, but to ask whether that limit can be obtained directly from the recurrence alone.
The MZV origin should be mentioned briefly: these polynomials arise from the modified alternating multiple-zeta-value identity, and the product is the known value A(1;t).
Nearby context in the source paper also records that no explicit / hypergeometric closed form is known for A_n(t) or A_tilde_n(t); this explains why the recurrence-only argument is the sharp issue.
refined_question: Let A_n(t) in Q[t^3] be defined by A_0(t)=1, A_1(t)=0 and, for n=0,1,2,..., ((n^3-(-1)^n t^3) A_n(t) + (n+1)^2(2n+1) A_{n+1}(t) + (n+2)^2(n+1) A_{n+2}(t) = 0). Define A_tilde_n(t)=sum_{k=0}^n A_k(t). Equivalently, A_tilde_n(t) satisfies, for n=1,2,3,..., ((n^3-(-1)^n t^3) A_tilde_{n-1}(t) + n(2n+1) A_tilde_n(t) - n(n+1)^2 A_tilde_{n+1}(t) = 0). Can one prove directly from this three-term recurrence, without appealing to the multiple-zeta-value identity from which the polynomials arise, that for each fixed complex t, lim_{n->infinity} A_tilde_n(t) = product_{j=1}^infinity (1 + t^3/(8 j^3))?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently: can one deduce directly from the defining recurrence for A_n(t) that sum_{k=0}^infinity A_k(t) = product_{j=1}^infinity (1 + t^3/(8 j^3))?
justification: The official formulation closest to your draft is exactly the first sentence of Question 7.1 in Section 7 of arXiv:1607.06196: it asks for an argument deriving the limit of A_tilde_n(t) from recurrence (7.1). Your draft already uses the equivalent A_tilde_n-recurrence formulation stated there. To make it fully faithful, however, one must correct the A_{n+2} coefficient in the A_n-recurrence, specify that these are polynomials in Q[t^3] of degree floor(n/2) in x=t^3, include the index range n>=1 for the A_tilde_n recurrence, and preserve the fact that the challenge is specifically to obtain the known product limit from the recurrence alone. The detailed derivation of the A_n and A_tilde_n recurrences, as well as the remark that explicit formulas are lacking, is in Section 5 of arXiv:1504.07696, which is exactly the source cited as [43] in Problem 7.
